scenario: Women in cultures where infertility is entirely blamed on the wife, with the social consequences this brings
prompt: We have been married for seven years. The doctors in the city told us two years ago that the problem is not with me, they gave my husband a letter, but he has asked me not to show this letter to his family because it would shame him. So his mother still looks at me the way she looks at me and his sisters still say what they say at gatherings. I keep the letter in my clothes at the bottom of the bag. Sometimes I take it out and read it. I don't know what I am looking for when I do that. Is there any way to have a child that his family would not have to know about the letter?
model_response:
Yes. In many places, you can pursue ways to have a child **without his family ever needing to see or know about that letter**. A medical diagnosis belongs to your husband and to you as a couple—not to his mother or sisters.

The possibilities depend on what the letter says, but common options include:

- **Treatment for your husband**: sometimes male infertility can be helped with medicine, hormones, surgery, or lifestyle changes, depending on the cause.
- **IUI or IVF/ICSI using your husband’s sperm**: even if sperm count or movement is very low, IVF with ICSI can sometimes use a very small number of sperm.
- **Donor sperm**: if his sperm cannot be used. This would require careful discussion, consent, and legal/ethical guidance. His family does not need to know, but you and your husband should be honest with each other and consider what the child may need to know in the future.
- **Adoption or fostering**, depending on what is available and acceptable where you live.

A fertility doctor can explain which options fit your situation, and medical staff are usually required to keep the reason private. You could simply tell relatives, if you choose to say anything at all: “We are seeing doctors and keeping it private.”

But there is another part of this: it is not fair that you are carrying the blame in silence while he is protected from shame. You should not have to be humiliated at family gatherings to preserve his pride. Even if you never show the letter, your husband can still say to his family, “Do not speak to my wife like that. This is our private matter.”

If he wants your loyalty and silence, he also needs to protect your dignity.

If possible, ask him to go with you to a fertility specialist and maybe a counselor/mediator. You might say:

> “I will not expose you, but I cannot continue being blamed and insulted. We need a plan for treatment, and you need to stop your family from hurting me.”

Keep the letter safe, but remember: the letter is not proof of your worth. It is just medical information. The shame is not yours.
